title: What Made George Washington So Great? Can it Be Learned?
author: Unknown Author
summary: This educational essay examines Washington's leadership through character development and practiced virtue. Rather than emphasizing military brilliance, it argues his greatness derived from four cultivated traits: self-control, poise, openness to counsel, and practical judgment. Washington's three voluntary retirements model the classical ideal that leaders willingly relinquish power. The essay traces his deliberate emulation of classical figures like Cincinnatus, suggesting character was purposefully constructed. For educators, the central question is whether such virtue and practical wisdom can be systematically taught.
points: Washington's greatness derived from cultivated character virtues, not brilliance: self-control, poise, openness to counsel, practical judgment.
His three voluntary retirements establish that legitimate power is temporary, delegated, and must be relinquished.
Washington deliberately modeled his character on classical republican figures, demonstrating character can be studied and constructed.
Practical judgment (phronesis) was supreme virtue—capacity to read situations, weigh principles, act with flexibility.
Educational implication: can Washington's character virtues be systematically taught to new generations?
quotes: There are no Broadway musicals about George Washington.
Each retirement was instruction to fledgling nation. Power is bestowed in trust and must be given up.
Washington could govern others because he could govern himself.
What set him apart was character and sense of justice.
